label: Reversible rule 37R does not obey the Second Law
claim: The reversible cellular automaton rule 37R, even as a closed system, shows neither a systematic trend toward increasing randomness nor simple predictable behavior, but fluctuates indefinitely between more and less ordered states, so it does not obey the Second Law for practical purposes.
quote: There is, I believe, no choice but to conclude that for practical purposes rule 37R simply does not obey the Second Law.
section: Irreversibility and the Second Law of Thermodynamics
scope: the second-order reversible elementary cellular automaton rule 37R in finite closed regions

label: Biological order arises from partitioning into separated compartments
claim: Biological systems can show increasing order despite the Second Law mainly because they partition into parts (cells, organisms) separated by membrane-like boundaries, within which organized behavior can occur while the boundary survives.
quote: This basic mechanism may well be the main one at work in many biological systems: each cell or each organism becomes separated from others, and while it survives, it can exhibit organized behavior.
section: Irreversibility and the Second Law of Thermodynamics
scope: biological systems exhibiting self-organization

label: The Second Law is general but not universally valid
claim: The Second Law of Thermodynamics is an important and general principle but is not universally valid; many systems in nature behave like rule 37R and do not show a uniform trend toward increasing randomness.
quote: And indeed I strongly suspect that there are many systems in nature which behave in more or less the same way. The Second Law is an important and quite general principle—but it is not universally valid.
section: Irreversibility and the Second Law of Thermodynamics
scope: physical, biological and other natural systems to which the Second Law is applied

label: Continuum behavior emerges from discrete randomizing conserving rules
claim: Smooth continuum behavior, such as diffusion of density, emerges from discrete systems whenever small-scale apparent randomness washes out individual details and conserved quantities constrain overall features, as shown by block cellular automata whose average density follows the diffusion equation.
quote: And much as in physical systems like fluids, what ultimately leads to this is the presence of small-scale apparent randomness that washes out details of individual cells or molecules—as well as of conserved quantities that force certain overall features not to change too quickly.
scope: discrete systems with conserved quantities and intrinsic randomness, such as particle-conserving block cellular automata and fluids

label: The fundamental rule cannot be found by working backwards from known laws
claim: If the ultimate rule for the universe is simple, it cannot realistically be found by engineering it from observed features; the only practical method is to choose a straightforward representation and systematically search through large numbers of candidate rules.
quote: my guess is that the only realistic way to find the rule in the first place will be to start from some very straightforward representation, and then just to search through large numbers of possible rules in this representation.
scope: methodology for finding a fundamental theory of physics

label: Space, gravity and quantum features are generic across many candidate rules
claim: Features such as seemingly continuous space and certain aspects of gravitation and quantum mechanics will emerge from many different underlying rules for the universe, whereas properties like the spectrum of particle masses, and perhaps the dimensionality of space, will be specific to particular rules.
quote: so also I suspect that properties such as the existence of seemingly continuous space, as well as certain features of gravitation and quantum mechanics, will emerge with many different possible underlying rules for the universe.
scope: candidate fundamental rules for the universe

label: Most known physical laws are emergent, not fundamental
claim: Most physical laws discovered so far are not fundamental but are emergent large-scale features of an underlying rule, so their simplicity says little about the simplicity of that rule.
quote: I strongly suspect that the vast majority of physical laws discovered so far are not truly fundamental, but are instead merely emergent features of the large-scale behavior of some ultimate underlying rule.
scope: known laws of physics

label: Space is discrete below the scales probed by experiment
claim: Space, though experimentally continuous down to about 10^-20 meters, is very likely made of discrete elements at still smaller scales, just as fluids and other seemingly continuous things have turned out to be.
quote: Particle physics experiments have shown that space acts as a continuum down to distances of around 10^(-20) meters—or a hundred thousandth the radius of a proton. But there is absolutely no reason to think that discrete elements will not be found at still smaller distances.
scope: the structure of physical space at very small distances

label: Space and matter should be made of the same stuff
claim: In the simplest ultimate model of the universe there is no distinction between space and its contents: matter and everything else are made of the same underlying structure as space, unlike in a cellular automaton.
quote: But if the ultimate model for the universe is to be as simple as possible, then it seems much more plausible that both space and its contents should somehow be made of the same stuff—so that in a sense space becomes the only thing in the universe.
scope: fundamental structure of space and matter

label: At the lowest level space is a network of nodes
claim: At the lowest level, space is most likely a giant network of nodes defined only by their connections (and it suffices to consider nodes with exactly three connections), with ordinary space emerging as a large-scale limit.
quote: And with this in mind I believe that what is by far the most likely is that at the lowest level space is in effect a giant network of nodes.
scope: fundamental structure of physical space

label: Network dimension is set by growth of node counts with distance
claim: A network corresponds to ordinary d-dimensional space exactly when the number of nodes within graph distance r of a node grows in a limiting sense like r^d; tree-like or randomly connected networks correspond to no finite dimension.
quote: in general the condition for a network to correspond to ordinary d-dimensional space is precisely that the total number of nodes that appear in it out to distance r grows in some limiting sense like r^d
scope: large networks and their correspondence to finite-dimensional space

label: Observers perceive time only through the causal network of events
claim: An observer embedded in a system such as a mobile automaton cannot see its individual update steps; all the observer can perceive is the network of causal relationships between updating events, so perceived time and spacetime derive purely from that causal network, and sequential updating can appear as synchronized parallel evolution.
quote: The most they will be able to tell is that a certain network of causal relationships exists—and their perception of time must therefore derive purely from the properties of this network.
scope: observers embedded in discrete evolving systems, including the universe

label: Non-overlapping replacement rules give update-order-independent causal networks
claim: A substitution system whose rules replace only blocks that can never overlap themselves or each other always yields the same causal network regardless of the order in which replacements are applied (the property Wolfram calls causal invariance).
quote: And any substitution system whose rules specify replacements only for blocks such as these is guaranteed to yield the same causal network regardless of the order in which replacements are performed.
section: The Sequencing of Events in the Universe
scope: string substitution systems and, analogously, network rewriting systems

label: The universe's rules likely yield a unique causal network
claim: Although the universe has no global clock and its rules may be applicable in arbitrary order, its actual rules most likely have the property of always yielding the same causal network, and so a unique perceived history.
quote: it still tends to be my suspicion that there is not—and that in fact the particular rules followed by the universe do in the end have the property that they always yield the same causal network.
scope: the fundamental update rules of the universe

label: Small-scale randomness in the network makes space robustly 3D
claim: The ultimate rules for the universe will produce networks that look largely random at small scales, and this randomness is what allows a definite and robust dimensionality of 3 to emerge for space.
quote: my expectation is that they will give rise to networks that on a small scale look largely random. But this very randomness will most likely be what for example allows a definite and robust value of 3 to emerge for the dimensionality of space
scope: network models of space and the dimensionality of physical space

label: Elementary length and time are tiny and their ratio is light speed
claim: Each connection in the causal network of the universe corresponds to an identical elementary distance (perhaps about 10^-35 meters) and elementary time (perhaps about 10^-43 seconds), whose ratio is a fixed speed identified with the speed of light.
quote: One may guess that this elementary distance is around 10^(-35) meters, and that the elementary time interval is around 10^(-43) seconds. But whatever these values are, a crucial point is that their ratio must be a fixed speed, and we can identify this with the speed of light.
scope: discrete structure of spacetime

label: Causal invariance yields special relativity
claim: If the underlying rules of the universe are causal invariant, then slices through the causal network at different angles, corresponding to different uniform velocities, are all governed by the same rules, so physics is the same regardless of uniform motion and the standard phenomena of special relativity such as time dilation follow.
quote: And the crucial point is that whenever the underlying system is causal invariant the exact same underlying rules will account for what one sees in slices at different angles. And what this means is that in effect the same rules will apply regardless of how fast one is going.
scope: discrete causal network models of spacetime and special relativity

label: Elementary particles are persistent localized structures in the network
claim: Elementary particles are analogs of the localized structures seen in class 4 cellular automata: persistent structures (such as tangles or non-planar cores) in the network of space, so that the fundamental rules need make no reference to particular particles.
quote: An immediate possibility that I suspect is actually not too far from the mark is that such particles are analogs of the localized structures that we saw earlier in this book in systems like the class 4 cellular automata shown below.
scope: elementary particles of physics

label: Fundamental particle masses may still have simple ratios
claim: Although observed elementary particle masses are not in simple ratios (unlike electric charges), truly fundamental particle masses may still have simple relations, because observed masses include varying amounts of interaction energy.
quote: But despite such results, it is still conceivable that there could in the end be simple relations between truly fundamental particle masses—since it turns out that the masses that have actually been observed in effect also include varying amounts of interaction energy.
scope: masses of elementary particles such as leptons and quarks

label: Network curvature appears in node counts via the Ricci scalar
claim: In a large network approximating d-dimensional space, the leading correction to the number of nodes reached within distance r is proportional to the Ricci scalar curvature times r^(d+1), so curvature can be determined purely from network connectivity.
quote: But in fact the leading correction to the number of nodes reached is always quite simple: it is just proportional to what is called the Ricci scalar curvature, multiplied by r^(d + 1).
scope: large networks approximating curved Riemannian spaces

label: Causal invariant dimension-preserving network rules give Einstein equations
claim: Network replacement rules that are causal invariant and maintain a fixed number of dimensions will almost inevitably produce large-scale behavior close to the vacuum Einstein equations of general relativity, analogous to how Navier–Stokes behavior emerges from cellular automaton fluids.
quote: But I suspect that if one has replacement rules that are causal invariant and that in effect successfully maintain a fixed number of dimensions they will almost inevitably lead to behavior that follows something close to the Einstein equations.
scope: causal invariant network rewriting systems and general relativity

label: Network-based programs will reproduce the key features of quantum theory
claim: Discrete network models of the universe with causal invariance will ultimately turn out to exhibit many if not all of the key features of quantum theory, even though they are not set up in terms of its standard formalism.
quote: And in fact it is my strong suspicion that the kinds of programs that I have discussed in the past few sections will actually in the end turn out to show many if not all the key features of quantum theory.
scope: network models of the universe and quantum phenomena

label: Network threads let deterministic models produce quantum correlations
claim: The quantum correlations between distant particles usually taken to rule out definite underlying processes can arise in a deterministic network model, because particles created together stay linked by threads of connections that bypass ordinary three-dimensional space.
quote: And the basic reason for this is that if the universe is a network then it can in a sense easily contain threads that continue to connect particles even when the particles get far apart in terms of ordinary space.
scope: correlations in measurements on entangled particle pairs (Bell-type experiments)

label: Perception and analysis are themselves carried out by simple programs
claim: The basic mechanisms underlying human perception and scientific analysis, like the mechanisms behind many natural processes, can be captured by simple programs based on simple rules.
quote: the evidence we have suggests that the basic mechanisms at work can once again successfully be captured by simple programs based on simple rules.
scope: human perception and methods of mathematical, statistical and computational analysis

label: Recovering a simple rule from its complex output is usually very hard
claim: Although inferring the generating procedure from observed behavior is fairly easy for the rules of traditional mathematics, for general simple programs it is often extremely difficult, because their complex output shows no obvious trace of its simple origin.
quote: But for the more general rules that I discuss in this book it appears to often be extremely difficult. For even though the rules may be simple, the behavior they produce is often highly complex, and shows absolutely no obvious trace of its simple origins.
scope: inference of generating rules from the output of cellular automata and other simple programs

label: Randomness cannot usefully be defined only by the existence of short descriptions
claim: Defining something as random only when no short description of it exists at all is too restrictive and uncomputable (it would mean deterministic rules can never generate randomness), so any useful definition of randomness must refer to how short descriptions are to be found.
quote: Indeed, what I suspect is that ultimately no useful definition of randomness can be based solely on the issue of what short descriptions of something may in principle exist.
scope: definitions of randomness, including description-length (algorithmic) definitions

label: Something is random if essentially no simple program detects regularities in it
claim: Since essentially all standard methods of perception and analysis are based on simple programs, something should be considered random whenever essentially no simple program succeeds in detecting regularities in it.
quote: something should be considered to be random whenever there is essentially no simple program that can succeed in detecting regularities in it.
scope: the definition of randomness for data of any kind

label: If a few standard tests find no regularity, other simple programs rarely do
claim: Once a few simple programs corresponding to standard methods of perception and analysis have failed to detect regularities in some data, it is extremely rare for any other simple program to succeed, so the everyday judgment of randomness is in practice fairly unambiguous.
quote: For once a few simple programs corresponding to a few standard methods of perception and analysis have failed to detect regularities, it is extremely rare for any other simple program to succeed in detecting them.
scope: detection of regularities in sequences and images by simple programs

label: Complexity means our perception and analysis fail to find a short description
claim: To call something complex is to say that our methods of perception and analysis have failed to find a short description of the features of it that we are interested in; complexity therefore depends on which features one chooses to capture.
quote: when we say that something seems complex, what we are effectively saying is that our powers of perception and analysis have failed on it.
scope: the definition of complexity

label: Most engaging images mix simply describable and indescribable features
claim: People tend to lose interest in images with no simple features (such as perfectly random ones), and the images that hold attention and seem most aesthetically pleasing are those in which some features are simple to describe while others have no short description findable by human visual perception.
quote: the images that draw us in the most—and typically that we find the most aesthetically pleasing—are those for which some features are simple for us to describe, but others have no short description that can be found by any of our standard processes of visual perception.
scope: human visual attention and aesthetic preference for images

label: Data compression methods all compress repetition and nesting but little else
claim: Structurally different lossless data compression methods (run-length, block/Huffman, pointer-based and two-dimensional schemes) have remarkably similar capabilities: they compress uniform regions, repetitive behavior and to some extent nested behavior, but achieve no substantial compression of more complex behavior even when it is generated by very short programs.
quote: Essentially every method, for example, will successfully compress large regions of uniform color. And most methods manage to compress behavior that is repetitive, and at least to some extent behavior that is nested—exactly the two kinds of simple behavior that we have noted many times in this book.
scope: lossless data compression algorithms applied to patterns from simple programs

label: Complex images lose recognizable features under lossy compression
claim: Under lossy compression by keeping only some basic forms (as in JPEG-like schemes), the relevant features of both simple and completely random images remain recognizable at high compression, whereas images normally considered complex need much lower compression, and reordering the basic forms does not change this substantially.
quote: But images that one would normally consider complex tend to have features that cannot be recognized except at significantly lower levels of compression.
scope: lossy transform-based image compression of simple, random and complex images

label: Texture is perceived through densities of simple local features
claim: Human perception generally works by cells responding to specific fixed features and ignoring others; in vision, cortical cells act as templates for small local patterns, and textures are distinguished by the densities of such local features, much as colors are distinguished by densities of red, green and blue.
quote: I strongly suspect that it is density differences such as these that allow our visual system to distinguish textures.
scope: human visual texture perception

label: Human vision easily detects repetition but generally fails to detect nesting
claim: Humans can readily see by eye that a two-dimensional pattern is purely repetitive, but generally cannot tell that a pattern is nested (unless it is dominated by large uniform areas), even though a simple two-dimensional pointer-based encoding recognizes the nesting.
quote: it is remarkably difficult for us to tell that the patterns are nested. And this can be viewed as a clear example of a limitation in our powers of visual perception.
scope: human visual recognition of repetitive and nested two-dimensional patterns

label: Hearing detects repetition at definite frequencies and essentially nothing else
claim: For sounds generated from sequences with fairly uniform properties, the human auditory system recognizes only exact or approximate repetition at definite frequencies; nested or other non-repetitive structure, beyond a few large spectral peaks, is heard as random noise.
quote: we readily recognize exact or approximate repetition at definite frequencies, and essentially nothing else.
scope: human auditory perception of sounds generated from discrete sequences

label: Best-fit probabilistic models of deterministic data look more random than the data
claim: When probabilistic models such as block-frequency, Markov or probabilistic cellular automaton models are fitted to data generated by deterministic cellular automata, they reproduce the statistics used in fitting but their typical behavior is considerably more random and misses most detailed features of the data.
quote: In most cases, the typical behavior produced by the model looks considerably more random than the data.
scope: statistical modeling of data generated by deterministic simple programs

label: Equal block frequencies of all lengths is not a universal randomness test
claim: Checking that all blocks of all lengths occur with equal frequency does not guarantee absence of regularity: sequences such as linear feedback shift register output or concatenated binary digits of successive integers have accurate block frequencies yet are non-random, as revealed for instance by an abnormally small spread of those frequencies.
quote: it has sometimes been thought that if one could just compute frequencies of blocks of all lengths one would have a kind of universal test for randomness. But sequences like (e) and (f) on the facing page make it clear that this is not the case.
scope: block-frequency tests for randomness of binary sequences

label: Rule 30 center column and digits of pi pass statistical tests for randomness
claim: The center column of the rule 30 cellular automaton and the base 2 digits of pi show no detectable deviation from randomness under block-frequency statistics or under analysis by simple cellular automata, even though both are generated by simple rules.
quote: statistical analysis, even with some generalization, cannot readily recognize that sequences like (g) and (h) are anything but completely random—even though at an underlying level these sequences were generated by quite simple rules.
scope: the rule 30 center-column sequence and the binary expansion of pi

label: Rule 30 can serve as a cryptographic stream cipher as secure as any known
claim: Simple rules with complex behavior, such as the rule 30 cellular automaton sampled sparsely to give an encrypting sequence, can be used to build stream ciphers at least as secure against cryptanalysis as any known system, unlike additive cellular automata or linear feedback shift registers, whose keys are easily recovered.
quote: I strongly suspect that they can, and that in fact they allow one to construct systems that are at least as secure to cryptanalysis as any that are known.
scope: stream ciphers based on cellular automata, specifically rule 30

label: Every nested pattern likely has a formula in generalized hypergeometric functions
claim: Although most nested patterns have no obvious relation to ordinary mathematical functions, a formula for the color of each cell of any nested pattern can probably be found in terms of suitably generalized hypergeometric functions or similar generalizations of traditional functions.
quote: it is my guess that in the end it will in fact turn out to be possible to get a formula for any nested pattern in terms of suitably generalized hypergeometric functions
scope: nested patterns generated by substitution systems

label: No simple formula describes many steps of rule 30 evolution
claim: Minimal Boolean formulas (in disjunctive normal form or in Nand operations) for the outcome of rule 30 grow rapidly with the number of steps, unlike those for simple rules such as 90 and 254, indicating that no simple formula describes rule 30 evolution and that, in most cases, cellular automaton patterns have no simple mathematical formula.
quote: So even if one allows rather general structure, the evidence is that in the end there is no way to set up any simple formula that will describe the outcome of evolution for a system like rule 30.
scope: formula representations of cellular automaton evolution, especially rule 30

label: Human memory works like similarity-preserving hashing by layers of neurons
claim: Human memory likely retrieves data by a simple hashing-like mechanism in which successive layers of nerve cells, each responding to patterns in fixed random sets of inputs, produce representations that are the same for inputs differing by small changes, allowing retrieval by similarity.
quote: this basic mechanism provides a simple way to get a representation—and thus a hash code—that will tend to be the same for pieces of data that somehow have enough features that are similar.
scope: mechanisms of human memory storage and retrieval

label: Memory retrieval, not logic, underlies almost all of human thinking
claim: Retrieval from memory on the basis of similarity underlies almost every major aspect of human thinking, including generalization, analogy and intuition, and logical reasoning is not fundamental but is itself carried out by retrieving learned patterns of argument from memory.
quote: My strong suspicion is that the use of memory is what in fact underlies almost every major aspect of human thinking.
scope: human cognition

label: The core of human thinking is based on rather simple rules
claim: Despite the complicated construction of the brain, there is a core to human thinking that is largely independent of neural details and is based on rather simple rules, with nothing fundamentally special about the processes involved.
quote: I strongly suspect that there is a definite core to the phenomenon of human thinking that is largely independent of such details—and that will in the end turn out to be based on rules that are rather simple.
scope: human thinking and its emulation by artificial systems

label: General human-like thinking is easier to reproduce than task-specific versions
claim: Because complex behavior from simple rules is hard to direct to specific tasks, it will likely be much easier to reproduce general human-like thinking than a special version of human-like thinking restricted to specific tasks; a recognizably human-like system would also need a human-like base of experience.
quote: most likely it will at some level be much easier to reproduce general human-like thinking than to set up some special version of human-like thinking only for specific tasks.
scope: artificial intelligence and emulation of human thinking

label: No method of perception or analysis can recognize all possible regularities
claim: No method of perception and analysis, however advanced, can in complete generality recognize all possible regularities and thus tell immediately whether a piece of data can be generated from some simple description, although higher methods could recognize some regularities current methods miss.
quote: My strong belief—as I will argue in Chapter 12—is that at least in complete generality this will never be possible.
section: Higher Forms of Perception and Analysis
scope: all possible methods of perception and analysis
